What is an Intent Object in CHATR?

An Intent Object is the sole unit of state managed by the CHATR Intent Kernel. Every Intent Object has required fields: id (UUID v4), version (semver), user_text (verbatim original utterance), capability (domain.verb format), lifecycle (phase + condition), policy, stewardship (when in STEWARDED phase), history (append-only event log), created_at and updated_at (ISO 8601 UTC). Intent Objects must survive kernel restarts, are stored in the stewarded_intents table, and are never physically deleted — they become read-only when ARCHIVED.

What are the lifecycle phases of a CHATR Intent Object?

A CHATR Intent Object progresses through these lifecycle phases: CREATED → PLANNED → EXECUTING → STEWARDED (for recurring intents) → ARCHIVED. Key invariants: lifecycle.phase is always present. lifecycle.condition is always present except when phase is ARCHIVED. The kernel lifecycle guard enforces all legal and forbidden transitions. Goals survive application restarts — the StewardshipRuntime restores all STEWARDED intents on kernel restart.

What are CHATR's 24 OS Principles?

CHATR's OS Principles include: Kernel owns goals. Workflows are attempts, not goals. Providers execute; kernel decides. Strategies choose how to pursue a capability. Ontology classifies; planner never classifies. Industries are data; capabilities are runtime. Execution never implies completion. Verification decides completion. Everything important is observable. Everything long-running is resumable. Everything consequential emits events. Every external action is policy checked. Every provider is trusted by evidence, not by presence. Every credential belongs to Identity and Secrets services. Every scarce resource is leased and scheduled. Agents propose; kernel decides and executes. Memory improves behavior, but never bypasses policy. World State represents observed reality, not ontology. Knowledge explains the world; World State tracks the world. Goals survive application restarts. Kernel services are shared infrastructure. Every public contract is versioned. ABI v1.0 freezes only after implementation evidence. Architecture changes are governed by ADRs, not tribal knowledge.

What are CHATR's Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)?

CHATR's ADRs govern architectural decisions. Key ADRs include: ADR-001: Goal-Oriented Not Workflow-Oriented — CHATR manages goals, not workflows. ADR-002: Universal Capabilities — capabilities are universal, not industry-specific. ADR-003: Industries Never Enter Kernel Runtime — industry data stays out of the kernel. ADR-004: Manifest-Driven Providers — providers are declared via manifests, not code. ADR-005: Goal Runtime Exists — a dedicated runtime stewards long-running goals. ADR-006: Verification Gates Completion — execution does not imply completion. ADR-007: Strategy Separate From Capability — how to pursue a goal is separate from the goal. ADR-008: Kernel Computed Trust — trust is computed by the kernel, not asserted by providers.

What is the CHATR Execution Definition Language (EDL)?

The Execution Definition Language (EDL) is CHATR's schema language for defining domain objects with their properties, lifecycle states, transitions, and event emissions. EDL schemas are defined as JSON files. An EDL object specifies: urn (unique resource name), type, primitiveType, properties (with type and required flags), relationships, lifecycle (initialState, states, transitions with triggeredByEvent and requiredPolicies), and eventsProduced. Examples include Candidate, Aircraft, Decision, and MaintenanceWorkOrder.

It has a relationship: assigned_to authority Employee (required, single). Lifecycle: applied → screening → interview → offer → hired (or rejected from any state). Transitions are triggered by events: CandidateScreeningStarted, CandidateInterviewScheduled, CandidateOffered (requires urn:chatr:policy:background-check), CandidateHired, CandidateRejected. Events produced: CandidateCreated, CandidateTransitioned.
